subject: Mathematics
central_question: How can a real-life optimisation problem with two decision variables and linear constraints be formulated and solved graphically?
in_scope_units: 12.1 Introduction: optimisation problems and the role of linear programming.
12.2 Linear Programming Problem and its Mathematical Formulation: decision variables, resource constraints and objective functions.
12.2.1 Mathematical Formulation of the Problem: translating the furniture-dealer situation into inequalities and a profit function.
12.2.2 Graphical Method of Solving Linear Programming Problems: feasible region, feasible and infeasible solutions, bounded and unbounded regions, corner-point theorems and the Corner Point Method.
Bounded optimisation examples for maximum, minimum and multiple optimal solutions.
Unbounded feasible regions and tests for the existence of an optimum.
Inconsistent constraints leading to no feasible region and no feasible solution.
Exercise 12.1 and the chapter summary and historical note.
banned_topics: Simplex method as a worked solution procedure, because the supplied chapter explicitly uses the graphical method only
Linear programming in three or more decision variables
Nonlinear objective functions or nonlinear constraints

known_pitfalls.claim: The objective function is one of the constraints.
known_pitfalls.correction: The objective function is the linear expression to maximise or minimise; constraints restrict the allowable values of the decision variables.

known_pitfalls.claim: Only points strictly inside the shaded region are feasible.
known_pitfalls.correction: Points inside and on the boundary of the feasible region are feasible solutions.

known_pitfalls.claim: The largest or smallest corner-point value is always the optimum even for an unbounded region.
known_pitfalls.correction: For an unbounded region, an additional open-half-plane test is required because an optimum may not exist.

known_pitfalls.claim: If two corner points give the same optimum, only those two points are optimal.
known_pitfalls.correction: Every point on the line segment joining those corner points also gives the same optimal value.

known_pitfalls.claim: A graph must always contain a feasible region.
known_pitfalls.correction: The constraints may have no common point, giving no feasible region and hence no feasible solution.

recommended_example_progression: Start with the NCERT furniture-dealer problem in Sections 12.1-12.2.1 to formulate variables, constraints and the profit objective.
Use NCERT Example 1 for a bounded maximisation problem solved by the Corner Point Method.
Use NCERT Example 2 for a bounded minimisation problem.
Use NCERT Example 3 to demonstrate multiple optimal solutions along a boundary segment.
Use NCERT Examples 4 and 5 to contrast an unbounded problem with no minimum and an inconsistent problem with no feasible solution.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Exercise 12.1 contains ten graphical linear-programming problems covering maximisation, minimisation, multiple optima, unbounded regions and infeasible systems.
